summary:
Central Java is a province of Indonesia and a visitor there stands under Indonesia's national legal framework, which the sources record as containing no criminalisation of gender identity itself, no X marker on identity documents, and no legal recognition of same-sex marriage. No provision specific to Central Java that would alter that position for a visitor is documented in the sources.

The national penal code was passed by the House of Representatives on 6 December 2022, signed by President Joko Widodo, and took effect on 2 January 2026. It criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with penalties reported at up to two years' imprisonment under the framework and at up to one year where a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, but because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls within the outside-marriage restriction. Reporting indicates that prosecutions under this provision are selective rather than systematic. The United Nations and other international critics condemned the code for failing to accommodate protections and rights for LGBT individuals and for domestic partnerships.

Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run an outreach issuing identification papers (KTP) to transgender Indonesians. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, and the birth gender is printed on the card unless a court order was obtained beforehand. Electronic identity cards were issued to transgender people in nine provinces. A visitor's documents therefore follow the same two-descriptor system.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes are codified into law; commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy. The August 2026 feature carried by The Diplomat is titled to Indonesia's transgender community facing growing repression.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, and in Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025 and two men were flogged in January 2021; Aceh's punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Those provisions do not extend to Central Java, where a visitor remains under the national framework alone.
tangentialFactors:
The raid on the villa in the Puncak area on 22 June 2025 took place in the province immediately west of Central Java, close to the provincial border, and shows that morality enforcement of this kind operates in the surrounding region rather than only in distant provinces. The pattern of administrative action against transgender people is documented in Jakarta, where the Jakarta Social Agency has carried out raids on transgender women.

Transgender identity, known locally as waria, has long been part of Indonesian culture, which contrasts with the current direction of official policy and with the legislative restrictions in force. The 2023 penal code attracted international criticism, including from the United Nations, over its treatment of LGBT individuals and domestic partnerships.

The divergence within Indonesia is sharp: Aceh and South Sumatra criminalise same-sex sexual activity at provincial level while the national framework does not explicitly do so, and Aceh's religious-law punishments apply to any person present there. A visitor travelling onward from Central Java to either province moves into a materially different legal position.
localsOnly:
Transgender Indonesians can obtain identity papers through the Ministry of Home Affairs outreach running since June 2021. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are available, and the birth gender appears on the card unless a court order for a gender change was obtained first. Electronic identity cards were issued to transgender people in nine provinces.

Residents have no anti-discrimination protection at national level and no route to legal recognition of a same-sex partnership, since same-sex marriage is not permitted. The outside-marriage offence in the penal code in force since 2 January 2026 can be set in motion by a complaint from an immediate family member, which makes the mechanism dependent on family complaint rather than routine police initiative.

Waria remains an established part of Indonesian cultural life despite the repressive incidents recorded by the sources, including the raids carried out by the Jakarta Social Agency on transgender women. Official framing has hardened: the October 2025 presidential decree places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Central Java provincial regulation (perda) addressing gender identity, morality offences or LGBT conduct is identified in the sources, and none is recorded as absent either. Whether the province has its own instrument mirroring national morality provisions remains unresolved here.

Enforcement frequency in Central Java is not sourced. The documented raids, arrests and canings in the inventory occurred in West Java, Aceh, Jakarta and Bali, so their applicability to Central Java as a pattern of local policing is unverified rather than excluded.

The sources give two different penalty figures for the outside-marriage offence: up to two years' imprisonment in the framework material and up to one year where the complaint comes from an immediate family member in the penal-code material. Which figure governs a given charge is unresolved.

Whether prosecutions under the 2 January 2026 provision have been brought in Central Java is not stated in any source, and the claim that prosecutions are selective rests on reporting rather than on case-level data for this province.
